newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU leaders head for summit amid EMU pact woes.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders head for summit amid EMU pact woes.

text.p: European Union leaders were due to arrive in the Dutch capital late on Sunday for one of the most contentious summits in the bloc's 40-year history.

Called to agree a new EU treaty, signalling a safe, free and just Citizens' Europe, the two-day summit has been overshadowed by a rift between the bloc's two main motors, France and Germany, over how to proceed towards monetary union.

The traditional Franco-German alliance, which has powered the Union to the brink of economic and monetary union (EMU), has been damaged by a new socialist French government which, though committed to a single currency due to be launched in January 1999, wants a fundamentally new approach to monetary union.

The Amsterdam summit on Monday and Tuesday was supposed to ratify a stability pact, agreed after tough negotiations between France and Germany at the last EU summit in Dublin in December and designed to impose budgetary discipline on the euro-zone.
But French and German leaders meeting in Poitiers in western France on Friday failed to patch up a rift over the pact.

French premier Lionel Jospin, who has promised his voters more jobs and an end to an austerity programme aimed at putting France in the EMU vanguard, insists that economic growth and jobs must be given the same priority as the stability pact in any Amsterdam deal.

Germany, however, opposes costly job-creation schemes which, it argues, have in the past merely raised inflation and interest rates and failed to cut unemployment. Bonn believes that the way to fight joblessness is through structural reforms.
Both sides have played down talk of a serious schism, saying that a deal in Amsterdam was possible but would require concessions all round.

EU finance ministers were due to meet for an informal dinner at 9.00 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Sunday in Amsterdam's prestigious Amstel Hotel, with talks on how to resolve the Franco-German dispute expected to continue in the wings of Monday's summit.
"The Germans have understood they must make a step forward if they want things to advance and we have to do the same," French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Saturday.
"Mutual concessions are the very definition of co-operation between two countries. It's difficult, but things are moving and I hope we will reach agreement in Amsterdam."

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and Finance Minister Theo Waigel remained confident France would support an undiluted stability pact, predicting Jospin would retreat from demands to attach job-creation programmes to the pact.
Waigel, architect of the stability pact, said there was no rift over the pact and that Germany was just as committed to fighting unemployment.
"France and Germany will clearly be pulling together on the same rope in Amsterdam," Kinkel told Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's deputy Wolfgang Schaeuble told Der Spiegel magazine on Saturday that any delay in launching the euro could jeopardise the whole project and upset currency markets.

Opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine said the rapid introduction of the euro would ease unemployment in the bloc, which is currently running at over 18 million, but a poll of 1,000 Germans found 51 percent opposed to the single currency.

French and German officials have been working intensively through the weekend to bridge their differences and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, who hosts the Amsterdam summit, predicted a deal would be struck, but only after lengthy negotiations.
"The meeting will only last two days, but the second day will be a long one," he said as he toured a tented press village near the Dutch Central Bank where the summit will be held.
"I'm still perfectly hopeful it will be possible to come to further solutions. We have presented our (EU) presidency paper...and it is now being discussed in various capitals.
In Amsterdam, around 150 demonstrators clashed with police when a protest march by up to 50,000 Europeans against hardship wrought by the bloc's quest for monetary union turned violent.
A large group of mainly German radicals, anarchists and punks broke away from the march and tried in vain to storm the Central Bank building where the summit will be held.
They smashed office and shop windows, overturned a police vehicle and pelted riot police with stones in the city centre.

Organisers of the European Marches Against Unemployment, Poverty and Social Exclusion said the protesters earlier jammed the city's central Dam square and walked through the streets to send a message to EU leaders ahead of the summit.
